questions.q: Cleavage refers to:
options: Mitotic cleavage produces progressively smaller blastomeres
questions.explain: Cleavage is a series of mitoses starting soon after fertilization. The cells it produces are called blastomeres.

open.q: What is cleavage?

questions.q: During cleavage, the overall size of the embryo:
options: Remains nearly constant while blastomeres shrink
Increases tenfold by the morula stage
questions.explain: There is little growth between divisions, so each division roughly halves blastomere volume. The embryo as a whole stays about the size of the zygote, inside the zona pellucida.

open.q: During cleavage, what happens to the overall size of the embryo?

questions.q: The 2-cell stage is reached approximately:
questions.explain: The 2-cell embryo appears about 30 hours after fertilization, the 4-cell stage at roughly 40 hours, and a 12–16-cell morula by about day 3.

open.q: Approximately how long after fertilization is the 2-cell stage reached?

questions.q: Compaction (about the 8-cell stage) involves:
options: E-cadherin-mediated adhesion with tight and gap junctions
questions.explain: Blastomeres flatten against each other, polarize and form junctions. Compaction separates inside cells (future inner cell mass) from outside cells (future trophoblast).

open.q: What does compaction (about the 8-cell stage) involve?

questions.q: The cleaving zygote travels along the uterine tube mainly by:
questions.explain: The embryo has no motility of its own. Muscular peristalsis and beating cilia, with tubal fluid flow, carry it toward the uterus.

open.q: By what mechanism does the cleaving zygote travel along the uterine tube?

questions.q: The morula is best described as:
options: A solid ball of about 12–32 blastomeres
A hollow ball with a fluid-filled cavity
A two-cell embryo with polar bodies
questions.explain: The morula looks like a mulberry. The fluid-filled cavity appears later, converting it to a blastocyst.

open.q: Describe the morula.

questions.q: The morula enters the uterine cavity approximately:
questions.explain: The morula reaches the uterus about 3–4 days after fertilization.

open.q: On about which day does the morula enter the uterine cavity?

questions.q: Why does the zona pellucida persist throughout early cleavage?
options: Keeps the conceptus enclosed and prevents premature implantation in the tube
questions.explain: The zona is not shed until the blastocyst hatches (about day 5), by which time the embryo is in the uterus. Losing it early could allow implantation in the tube (ectopic pregnancy).

open.q: Why does the zona pellucida persist throughout early cleavage?

questions.q: Which statement about human cleavage is correct?
options: It is complete (holoblastic) and slow, with later divisions asynchronous
It is meroblastic, confined to a disc of cytoplasm
It is superficial, with nuclei dividing in shared yolk
It is rapid and perfectly synchronous up to the blastocyst
questions.explain: Human oocytes contain little yolk, so the whole zygote divides. Divisions are slow and become asynchronous after the 2-cell stage.

questions.q: The earliest cleavage divisions depend mainly on:
options: Maternal mRNA and proteins stored in the oocyte
questions.explain: The embryonic genome is switched on around the 4–8-cell stage, so earlier divisions rely on maternal stores.

open.q: What do the earliest cleavage divisions depend on mainly?

questions.q: Which sequence of week-1 events is correct?
options: Zygote → 2-cell → morula → blastocyst → hatching → start of implantation
questions.explain: Fertilization (day 0) → 2-cell (~30 h) → morula (day 3) → blastocyst (day 4–5) → hatching (day 5) → implantation begins (day 6).

open.q: List the week-1 sequence from zygote to the start of implantation.

questions.q: Which statement about blastomere potential is most widely accepted?
options: Blastomeres up to about the 8-cell stage are totipotent
Only inner cell mass cells are totipotent
Blastomeres commit to placenta or embryo at the 2-cell stage
questions.explain: Early blastomeres can each give rise to a complete embryo, which is why splitting at the 2-cell stage can produce monozygotic twins. Inner cell mass cells are pluripotent, not totipotent.

open.q: Up to about which stage are blastomeres considered totipotent?

questions.q: Which part of the blastocyst forms the embryo proper?
questions.explain: The inner cell mass (embryoblast) gives rise to the embryo. In week 2 it splits into epiblast and hypoblast.

open.q: Which part of the blastocyst forms the embryo proper?

questions.q: The outer cell layer of the blastocyst (trophoblast) contributes to:
options: The fetal part of the placenta (chorion)
questions.explain: The trophoblast forms the chorion and the fetal portion of the placenta, and it mediates implantation.

open.q: To what does the trophoblast (outer cell layer of the blastocyst) contribute?

questions.q: The blastocystic cavity forms when:
options: Fluid enters between morula cells through the zona pellucida
Inner cell mass cells undergo apoptosis
questions.explain: Fluid from the uterine cavity enters, spaces coalesce into one cavity, and the morula becomes a blastocyst (around day 4–5). The inner cells gather at one pole as the inner cell mass.

open.q: How does the blastocystic cavity form?

questions.q: The zona pellucida is shed ('hatching') at about:
questions.explain: Around day 5 the blastocyst frees itself from the zona. This exposes the trophoblast so it can attach to the endometrium.

open.q: On about which day is the zona pellucida shed ('hatching')?

questions.q: Implantation begins at about:
questions.explain: The blastocyst starts attaching to the endometrial epithelium around day 6, at the end of week 1. Implantation is completed during week 2.

open.q: Implantation begins at about which day?

questions.q: Which pole of the blastocyst attaches to the endometrium first?
options: Neither: it floats free until week 3
questions.explain: The trophoblast over the embryonic pole, next to the inner cell mass, adheres first.

open.q: Which pole of the blastocyst attaches to the endometrium first?

questions.q: Implantation occurs in the endometrium during the:
questions.explain: Progesterone from the corpus luteum prepares a secretory endometrium. The window of receptivity is roughly days 20–24 of a 28-day cycle.

open.q: During which phase of the endometrial cycle does implantation occur?

questions.q: The usual site of normal implantation is the:
options: Upper posterior wall of the uterine body
questions.explain: Implantation near the internal os predisposes to placenta previa. Implantation outside the uterus is ectopic.

open.q: What is the usual site of normal implantation?
accept: posterior wall of body of uterus

questions.q: Which cells secrete hCG?
questions.explain: The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer, multinucleated, invasive layer of the trophoblast that forms at implantation. hCG is the basis of pregnancy tests.

open.q: Which cells secrete hCG?

questions.q: The main role of hCG in early pregnancy is to:
options: Maintaining the corpus luteum and progesterone secretion
questions.explain: hCG acts like LH and keeps the corpus luteum secreting progesterone until the placenta takes over, at around weeks 8–10.

open.q: What is the main role of hCG in early pregnancy?

questions.q: At the start of implantation the trophoblast differentiates into:
options: An inner cytotrophoblast and an outer syncytiotrophoblast
A blastomere and a polar body
questions.explain: Cytotrophoblast is the inner, mitotically active layer. Syncytiotrophoblast is the outer, invasive, multinucleated layer. Epiblast and hypoblast come from the inner cell mass in week 2.

open.q: Into what does the trophoblast differentiate at the start of implantation?

questions.q: A 27-year-old with previous pelvic inflammatory disease has 6 weeks of amenorrhoea, unilateral lower abdominal pain and a positive pregnancy test. Where is the embryo most likely implanted?
options: Posterior wall of the uterine body
questions.explain: Tubal scarring slows transport, while the zona is shed on schedule (about day 5), so the blastocyst can implant in the tube. The ampulla is the most common ectopic site.

open.q: A 27-year-old with previous pelvic inflammatory disease has 6 weeks of amenorrhoea, unilateral lower abdominal pain and a positive pregnancy test. Where is the embryo most likely implanted?

questions.q: In IVF, blastocyst-stage embryos are usually transferred on about day:
questions.explain: Embryos are cultured to the blastocyst stage (about day 5) before transfer, which also lets the lab select the best-developing embryos.

open.q: In IVF, on about which day are blastocyst-stage embryos usually transferred?

questions.q: Why can a few trophectoderm cells be biopsied at the blastocyst stage for preimplantation genetic testing?
options: They contribute to placental tissues; the inner cell mass forms the embryo
They are totipotent and form the placenta
questions.explain: Trophectoderm is mostly extraembryonic, so removing a few cells leaves the inner cell mass that becomes the embryo.

open.q: Why can a few trophectoderm cells be biopsied at the blastocyst stage for preimplantation genetic testing?
accept: inner cell mass is left intact

questions.q: In a woman with a regular 28-day cycle, fertilization usually occurs about how long after the first day of her last menstrual period?
questions.explain: Gestational age is counted from the LMP, so it runs about 2 weeks ahead of fertilization age. A blastocyst starting to implant at fertilization age 1 week is at about gestational week 3.

open.q: In a regular 28-day cycle, fertilization usually occurs about how long after the first day of the last menstrual period?

questions.q: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception acts mainly by:
questions.explain: Taken before the LH surge, it delays ovulation so sperm and oocyte do not meet. It does not end an established pregnancy.

open.q: How does levonorgestrel emergency contraception act mainly?

questions.q: Which description fits a complete hydatidiform mole?
options: 46,XX with all chromosomes of paternal origin
46,XY with equal maternal and paternal contributions
questions.explain: An oocyte without a maternal nucleus is fertilized and the paternal haploid set duplicates. A partial mole is typically triploid (69) from dispermy.

open.q: Describe the chromosomes of a complete hydatidiform mole.

questions.q: On approximately which day after fertilization does the blastocyst normally begin attaching to and implanting into the endometrium?
questions.explain: After hatching from the zona pellucida around day 5, the blastocyst attaches to the endometrial epithelium by its embryonic pole on day 6 and completes interstitial implantation by day 10 to 12.

open.q: Around which day post-fertilization does the blastocyst initiate attachment and implantation into the uterine endometrium?

questions.q: In which part of the uterus does normal blastocyst implantation take place?
options: Lower uterine segment near the internal os
questions.explain: Normal implantation occurs in the functional layer of the endometrium along the superior posterior (most common) or anterior wall of the uterine body.

open.q: In which anatomical region of the uterus does normal blastocyst implantation occur?
accept: fundus or upper body of uterus

questions.q: Into which two layers does the trophoblast differentiate upon contact with the endometrial stroma during implantation?
questions.explain: At the embryonic pole, proliferating trophoblast cells divide into an inner mononucleated cytotrophoblast layer and an outer invasive, multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast that erodes endometrial glands and vessels and secretes hCG.

open.q: Name the two distinct trophoblastic layers formed at the embryonic pole as the blastocyst invades the endometrium.

questions.q: A 31-year-old multigravida in her third trimester presents with painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows the placenta completely covering the internal cervical os (placenta previa). Implantation in which uterine location predisposes to this condition?
options: Lower uterine segment near the internal os
questions.explain: Placenta previa results when the blastocyst implants low in the lower uterine segment near or over the internal cervical os rather than in the upper uterine body.

open.q: Blastocyst implantation in which region of the uterus leads to placenta previa?

questions.q: During the second week of development ('week of twos'), into which two epithelial layers does the embryoblast (inner cell mass) differentiate?
questions.explain: Around day 8, the embryoblast differentiates into a dorsal layer of tall columnar cells (epiblast) and a ventral layer of small cuboidal cells (hypoblast) facing the blastocyst cavity, forming the bilaminar embryonic disc.

open.q: Name the two cell layers of the bilaminar embryonic disc formed by the embryoblast during week 2.

questions.q: Within which layer of the bilaminar embryonic disc does the amniotic cavity first appear around day 8?
questions.explain: A small cleft appears between epiblast cells and enlarges into the amniotic cavity; epiblast cells adjacent to the cytotrophoblast differentiate into amnioblasts lining the roof of the amnion.

open.q: Within which layer of the bilaminar disc does the amniotic cavity initially cavitate during the second week?

questions.q: What is the exocoelomic (Heuser) membrane that lines the primary yolk sac derived from?
options: Hypoblast cells migrating around the blastocyst cavity
Epiblast cells migrating through the primitive streak
questions.explain: Flattened cells originating from the hypoblast delaminate and spread to line the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast, forming the exocoelomic (Heuser) membrane that encloses the primary yolk sac (exocoelomic cavity).

open.q: From which layer of the bilaminar disc do the flattened cells forming the exocoelomic (Heuser) membrane originate?

questions.q: When the extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity) expands and splits the extraembryonic mesoderm into two layers, what is the suspension bridge of extraembryonic mesoderm that attaches the bilaminar disc and amnion to the chorion called?
questions.explain: The extraembryonic coelom surrounds the amnion and secondary yolk sac everywhere except at the caudal region where the connecting stalk anchors the embryo to the trophoblast/chorion; this stalk later becomes the umbilical cord.

open.q: Name the band of extraembryonic mesoderm that suspends the embryo and its cavities within the chorionic cavity and later forms the umbilical cord.

questions.q: What are the three components that together form the chorion at the end of the second week?
options: Extraembryonic somatic mesoderm, cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast
Extraembryonic splanchnic mesoderm, yolk sac and allantois
questions.explain: The chorionic plate/wall consists of the outer syncytiotrophoblast, the middle cytotrophoblast, and the inner lining of extraembryonic somatic (somatopleuric) mesoderm.

open.q: List the three tissue layers that make up the chorion at the end of week 2.
accept: extraembryonic somatic mesoderm, cytotrophoblast, and syncytiotrophoblast
syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm

questions.q: What is the thickened circular area of columnar hypoblast cells at the cranial end of the bilaminar disc that establishes the cranial-caudal axis and forms the future buccopharyngeal (oropharyngeal) membrane?
questions.explain: The prechordal plate is a localized firm adhesion between cranial hypoblast and epiblast cells where no mesoderm intervenes, marking the site of the future mouth (oropharyngeal membrane) and organizing forebrain induction.

open.q: Name the cranial thickening of hypoblast tightly adherent to the overlying epiblast that marks the site of the future mouth.

questions.q: Which morphological structure appears on the caudal dorsal surface of the epiblast at the start of week 3 to initiate gastrulation?
questions.explain: Gastrulation begins around day 15 with the appearance of the primitive streak (a linear midline thickening of proliferating epiblast cells) at the caudal end of the embryonic disc.

open.q: Name the midline thickening of epiblast cells at the caudal end of the embryonic disc that initiates gastrulation in week 3.

questions.q: From which layer of the bilaminar embryonic disc do ALL three definitive intraembryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm) originate during gastrulation?
questions.explain: During gastrulation, epiblast cells migrate toward the primitive streak, invaginate through the primitive groove, displace the hypoblast to form definitive endoderm, populate the middle space as intraembryonic mesoderm, and remain on the surface as ectoderm.

open.q: Which single layer of the bilaminar disc gives rise to all three definitive embryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm)?

questions.q: Which two specialized midline regions of the trilaminar embryonic disc remain strictly bilaminar (ectoderm directly apposed to endoderm with NO intervening mesoderm)?
questions.explain: Migrating intraembryonic mesoderm spreads everywhere between ectoderm and endoderm except at the cranial oropharyngeal membrane and the caudal cloacal membrane, which later rupture to create the oral and urogenital/anal openings.

open.q: Name the two midline membranes of the embryonic disc where ectoderm and endoderm remain directly fused without intervening mesoderm.

questions.q: From which structure do epiblast cells ingress cranially to form the hollow notochordal process and ultimately the definitive solid notochord?
questions.explain: Epiblast cells invaginating through the primitive pit at the cranial end of the primitive streak (primitive node) migrate cranially in the midline to form the notochordal process, which folds into the solid notochord.

open.q: Through which specific cranial structure of the primitive streak do cells ingress to form the notochord?

questions.q: What is the sole adult anatomical remnant of the embryonic notochord in humans?
options: Nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs
Annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral discs
questions.explain: While the vertebral bodies and annulus fibrosus develop from sclerotome mesoderm surrounding the notochord, the notochord regresses within vertebral bodies and persists only as the mucoid nucleus pulposus at the center of each intervertebral disc.

open.q: Which central gelatinous component of the adult intervertebral disc represents the persistent remnant of the notochord?

questions.q: How does the notochord induce the overlying midline ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate during primary neurulation?
options: Notochordal BMP antagonists (noggin, chordin, follistatin) induce the neural plate
Surface ectoderm is removed by phagocytosis
questions.explain: In the absence of signaling, ectoderm defaults to neural fate when BMP4 is inhibited; the notochord and primitive node secrete noggin, chordin, and follistatin to neutralize BMP4 and induce neural plate formation.

open.q: Which signaling molecules secreted by the notochord and primitive node inhibit BMP4 to induce neural plate formation in overlying ectoderm?

questions.q: Which transient multipotent cell population detaches from the crests (lateral edges) of the neural folds as the neural tube closes and migrates throughout the embryo to form dorsal root ganglia, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, and craniofacial cartilage?
questions.explain: Neural crest cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition at the neuroectoderm-surface ectoderm border during neural tube closure, giving rise to PNS neurons/glia, melanocytes, chromaffin cells, and pharyngeal arch mesenchyme.

open.q: Name the migratory multipotent cell population arising from the dorsal margins of the closing neural folds that gives rise to PNS ganglia, melanocytes, and the adrenal medulla.

questions.sub: Week 3: Mesoderm Subdivision and Chorionic Villi
questions.q: Into which three longitudinal columns does intraembryonic mesoderm on either side of the notochord differentiate during week 3?
options: Paraxial mesoderm, intermediate mesoderm, and lateral plate mesoderm
questions.explain: From medial to lateral beside the neural tube and notochord, intraembryonic mesoderm organizes into paraxial mesoderm (forming somites), intermediate mesoderm (forming urogenital structures), and lateral plate mesoderm (splitting into somatic and splanchnic layers).

open.q: List the three longitudinal subdivisions of intraembryonic mesoderm from medial to lateral during week 3.
accept: paraxial, intermediate, and lateral plate mesoderm
paraxial mesoderm, intermediate mesoderm, lateral plate mesoderm

questions.sub: Week 3: Mesoderm Subdivision and Chorionic Villi
questions.q: What distinguishes a tertiary chorionic villus from a secondary chorionic villus during week 3?
options: Development of fetal blood capillaries within the mesenchymal villous core
Invasion of extraembryonic mesoderm into a primary cytotrophoblastic villus
Formation of maternal spiral arteries in the decidua
Complete disappearance of the cytotrophoblastic shell
questions.explain: Primary villi consist of a cytotrophoblast core covered by syncytiotrophoblast; secondary villi gain an inner core of extraembryonic mesoderm; tertiary (definitive) villi form by the end of week 3 when mesenchymal cells differentiate into fetal blood vessels.

open.q: Which structural addition converts a secondary chorionic villus into a tertiary chorionic villus by the end of week 3?
accept: blood vessels in the villous core

questions.sub: Week 3: Mesoderm Subdivision and Chorionic Villi
questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents at 10 weeks gestation with vaginal bleeding, a uterus much larger than expected for dates, markedly elevated serum hCG, and a 'snowstorm' ultrasound appearance with no fetus (complete hydatidiform mole). What is the typical chromosomal constitution of a complete mole?
options: 69,XXY with two maternal and one paternal sets
questions.explain: A complete hydatidiform mole typically has a 46,XX (occasionally 46,XY) karyotype in which all chromosomes are paternally derived (fertilization of an anucleate 'empty' ovum by one sperm that duplicates, or two sperm), driving exuberant trophoblastic proliferation without an embryo.

open.q: What is the parental origin of the diploid chromosome set in a complete hydatidiform mole?
